liegemen: sworn followers who owed loyal service to a lord
liegeman: a sworn follower bound to serve a particular lord
liegelord: the lord to whom a warrior owed loyalty and service
atheling: a prince or noble youth of royal blood
thane: a nobleman who served a king and held land from him
thanemen: the followers and companions of a thane
earlmen: noblemen or warriors of high rank
mead-hall: the great hall where warriors feasted and drank mead
mead-bench: a long bench in the mead-hall where feasters sat
bairn: a child, especially a young son or daughter
burnie: a coat of mail armor made of linked iron rings
corslet: a piece of body armor covering the chest and back
welkin: the sky or the heavens above
moor-fens: marshy wetlands and bogs on the open moors
wassail-hall: a hall where people gathered for drinking and festive feasting
eotens: giants, monstrous beings of old folklore and legend
direful: dreadful, terrible, causing great fear or horror
doughty: brave, bold, and valiant in the face of danger
gleeman: a minstrel who sang and recited poems for a hall's company
nickers: water monsters or sea-serpents living in lakes and seas
woful: full of sorrow; sad, wretched, or grieving
hither: to this place, toward the speaker
thence: from that place or from that point
thenceward: from that place, in that direction
afterward: later, after that time has passed
thereupon: immediately after that, as a result of this
requital: repayment or return for an injury or a favor
glimmer: a faint, unsteady light or gleam
ring-stemmed: having a curved prow ornamented with rings, as on a ship
holm-currents: currents of the open sea, the ocean's rolling streams
mere-ways: paths across the sea, the routes of ships
weltering: rolling and tossing violently, as with waves or blood
ring-mail: armor made of many small interlocking metal rings
war-burnie: a warrior's coat of mail worn into battle
battle-brave: brave and fearless when fighting in battle
strength-famous: renowned for great physical strength and power
proud-mooded: proud in spirit, haughty, and confident in bearing
march-stepper: a poetic term for a horse, a steed that paces lands
fastness: a fortified stronghold or secure hiding place
beaker: a drinking cup, often used at feasts
bosom: the chest, or the breast, the seat of feeling
scathers: those who harm or injure others; destroyers and enemies
folk-leader: the chief or ruler who leads a people or nation
bedmate: a spouse who shares one's bed
dynasty: a line of rulers from the same family
sooth: the truth, or what is actually true
fitts: the sections or cantos into which the poem is divided
alliteration: repetition of the same initial consonant sound in nearby words
stabreimend: German term meaning alliterating, using repeated initial sounds
übersetzt: German for translated, rendered from one language into another
emendations: corrections or improvements made to a text by an editor
uptowered: risen high, towering up into the air
uncanny: strange and eerie, seeming unnatural or supernatural
fuddled: confused or stupefied, especially from too much drink
weened: thought or supposed, believed in the mind
trappings: decorations or ornaments, especially on a horse or armor
gefrætwod: adorned or decorated with ornaments, Old English
eaxle: the shoulder, an Old English word for the body part
shalt: an archaic form meaning 'shall' used with 'thou'
mindful: aware of and remembering something important
heathen: a person who does not follow Christianity; a pagan
wielded: held and swung or used a weapon with skill
brandished: waved or shook a weapon threateningly in the air
hastened: hurried or moved quickly toward a place
utter: complete, total, absolute, without any exception
ne'er: a contraction of never, meaning at no time
fared: went or traveled, or got along in a situation
hringed: ringed or decorated with metal rings or bands
gearwe: ready or prepared for what was to come
